name: End-of-history illusion
statement: People of every age report having changed a lot over the past decade and expect to change little over the next one.
meaning: The claim has two halves that only look consistent from inside. Asked how much their personality, values or tastes shifted over the last ten years, people report a lot. Asked how much those things will shift over the next ten, the same sort of people report a little. Since everyone was once ten years younger, both answers cannot be right, and the label treats the forward-looking one as the mistake. That is a claim about prediction rather than about memory. It predicts something testable, which is that a person's forecast of their future self should fall short of what that person later turns out to be.

origin.who: Jordi Quoidbach, Daniel T. Gilbert and Timothy D. Wilson
origin.note: Their design compared predictors aged a with reporters aged a + 10, drawn from the same recruitment pool. Nobody was followed over ten years, so the gap in the analysis is a gap between people rather than a gap in anyone's life. Two follow-ups did let some participants answer in both conditions on the same day, which tests scale wording rather than the passage of time.

evidence: Six studies, four numbered and two follow-ups. In study 1, 7,519 adults aged 18 to 68 completed the Ten Item Personality Inventory, then rated themselves either as they had been ten years earlier or as they expected to be ten years later. The condition coefficient was b = -0.14, p < 0.001. Study 2 ran the same design on 2,717 adults using ten values from the Schwartz Value Inventory, b = -0.46, p < 0.001. Study 3 asked 7,130 adults about five concrete preferences, their favourite music, holiday, food and hobby and the name of their best friend, b = -0.19, p < 0.001. One follow-up on 613 adults put each person in both conditions and gave b = -7.69, p = 0.001. A second, on 1,163 adults, asked in one general question how much they had changed or would change, b = -0.74, p = 0.007. To test whether reporters were simply misremembering, the authors set intraclass correlations against 3,808 adults measured twice in the MacArthur Midlife Development survey. Actual change over the decade gave 0.52, reported change 0.51 and predicted change 0.65, and a larger correlation means less change. Study 4 randomly assigned 170 people on Mechanical Turk to one concert question or the other. Those asked about seeing their current favourite band in ten years named $129 on average, against $80 from participants a decade older asked about seeing their once-favourite band next week. The paper puts that at 61% more for the future concert.

examples.tag: The student who has finished changing
examples.text: A man of twenty describes how far his politics and his taste in music moved since school, then says he expects to hold much the same views at thirty. His account of the decade behind him is not the account he gives of the decade ahead.

examples.tag: The tattoo that will always mean this
examples.text: Someone choosing a design assumes the meaning it carries now is the meaning it will keep, while saying readily what the same design would have meant to them at school. Change is granted to the past and withheld from the future.

examples.tag: The cottage bought for the quiet
examples.text: A couple buy a house an hour from anyone, reasoning from the weekends they want now, having already remarked how far their idea of a good weekend has moved since their twenties. The forecast of change falls short of the change they report.

replication.headline: The one longitudinal test produced two papers reading the same data in opposite directions, and the disagreement is about whether change is counted with its sign.
replication.detail: Harris and Busseri tested the claim on life satisfaction across three waves of the MacArthur Midlife Development survey, which records both what people predicted and what later happened. They concluded that most individuals were accurate or expected too much change rather than too little. Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson re-analysed the same survey and concluded the opposite, reporting that predicted absolute change fell short of experienced absolute change, b = 0.15, t(10,430) = 8.463, p < 0.001, over 3,909 participants and 14,174 observations. That comment also records that its oldest participants, aged 75 and over, seem to have expected too much change rather than too little. Busseri and Harris then reproduced that result in their own 2,390-person subsample, b = 0.16, t(2,389) = 5.51, p < 0.001, with mean experienced change of 0.97 against mean predicted change of 0.82. They located the disagreement in the measure. Counted as absolute values the effect appears, yet only 36% of individuals predicted too little change, while 38% were accurate and 26% predicted too much. Counted with direction kept, b = 0.26, t(2,389) = 7.13, p < 0.001, and people in their thirties, forties and fifties expected too much improvement, those in their sixties were accurate, and those in their seventies expected too much decline. The pattern itself reappears in other cross-sectional designs. Children aged 4 to 11 show it between subjects (N = 178) and again within subjects (N = 82). Asked instead about other children of the same age, 83 children reversed it and expected others to change more in the future than in the past. Public service professionals randomised to report or predict show it for work motivations. Haas and Omura report the gap as larger among US Americans than among Japanese, for life satisfaction and personality traits, though only their abstract could be opened here.

study.cite: Harris, H., & Busseri, M. A. (2019). Is there an 'end of history illusion' for life satisfaction? Evidence from a three-wave longitudinal study. Journal of Research in Personality, 83, 103869.

limits: The 2013 design is cross-sectional and the claim is developmental. A 33-year-old's forecast was set against a 43-year-old's recollection, so cohort differences and errors of prediction cannot be separated. The paper states no such caveat. In their 2020 comment the same three authors list their own 2013 studies among work 'limited by the use of retrospective or peer-reports rather than directly measuring change'. The only limitation the 2013 supplement raises is that too few older participants took part to say whether the illusion survives at the top of the age range. Over 80% of participants in studies 1 to 3 were women, recruited through the website of a French television programme. The MacArthur comparison used a different scale from the authors' own, and they say direct comparison of the data was not possible. All the longitudinal work covers life satisfaction on one item, a 0 to 10 ladder asked at three waves, not personality, values or preferences. Harris and Busseri record that their hypotheses and methods were not preregistered, and the study on children says the same of itself. No preregistered replication of the 2013 protocol was found on 21 September 2026. PubMed returns eight records for the phrase and none is one, Crossref adds only a data deposit and a textbook chapter, and no technical comment on the Science paper appears in either.
misreadings: The 2013 studies cannot show that anybody was wrong about the future, because no future was measured. They show that forecasts collected at one age are smaller than recollections collected at another. The nearest thing to an accuracy test in the paper compares two different samples on two different scales, which is why the authors report intraclass correlations rather than a difference. The 19,000 figure covers six studies; the largest single sample is 7,519 and the concert result rests on 170 people. The finding is also not that people expect to stop changing. Predicted change was smaller than reported change, not zero. And the version of the claim that survives longitudinal data is about absolute magnitude. Restore the sign and the same records show adults in their thirties, forties and fifties expecting too much improvement, which is the opposite error from expecting too little change.

sources.text: Quoidbach, J., Gilbert, D. T., & Wilson, T. D. (2013). The end of history illusion. Science, 339(6115), 96-98. Read in full, article and supplement together, from the copy on the corresponding author's Harvard page, and checked against a second copy held by the MIDUS project. Every 2013 figure on this page was found in that text.

Harris, H., & Busseri, M. A. (2019). Is there an 'end of history illusion' for life satisfaction? Evidence from a three-wave longitudinal study. Journal of Research in Personality, 83, 103869. Read from the open copy the MIDUS project hosts, which the publisher's own site does not serve. The sample of 2,390, the single-item ladder and the accuracy shares come from it.

Quoidbach, J., Gilbert, D. T., & Wilson, T. D. (2020). Your life satisfaction will change more than you think: A comment on Harris and Busseri (2019). Journal of Research in Personality, 86, 103937. Read from the MIDUS copy. The coefficient, the participant and observation counts and the quoted remark about retrospective reports were all found in it.

Busseri, M. A., & Harris, H. (2020). Life satisfaction and the 'end of history illusion': A reply to Quoidbach, Gilbert, and Wilson (2020). Journal of Research in Personality, 88, 104013. Read in full from the MIDUS copy. Note that the reply calls the directional difference negative while printing its coefficient unsigned, so the printed 0.26 carries the sign only in the surrounding sentence.

Sacchi, A., Sah, J., Finlay, M., & Starmans, C. (2024). Forever young: The end of history illusion in children. Cognition, 250, 105867. Read in full from the authors' laboratory copy at Toronto, reached on 21 September 2026 by solving the site's proof-of-work challenge. Its samples are 178, 82 and 83 children, and its third experiment reverses the effect rather than merely failing to find it.

Haas, B. W., & Omura, K. (2022). Cultural differences in susceptibility to the end of history illusion. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 48(9), 1331-1348. Abstract only, read from the PubMed record on 21 September 2026. Sage answers its own PDF route with a Cloudflare challenge rather than a paywall notice, and the article is absent from Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, CORE and the Wayback Machine. Its supplement sits on Sage's figshare portal, which returned 403. No figure from it is used here.

Van Ryzin, G. G. (2016). Evidence of an 'end of history illusion' in the work motivations of public service professionals. Public Administration, 94(1), 263-275. Abstract only, read from a 2021 Wayback capture of the publisher's page on 21 September 2026. Wiley answers its own PDF route with a Cloudflare challenge, and no repository copy was found. The design and the direction of its result come from that abstract, and no figure from it is used here.
